reforms.description: Japan launched the 2008 Cool Earth Promotion Programme, committing approximately $30 billion (0.6% of 2008 GDP) over five years for public R&D investment in climate and energy efficiency technologies to support the transition to a low-carbon society. The programme includes basic and applied research on climate-related technologies, technology transfer to developing countries via a multilateral fund contribution of up to $1.2 billion, and aims to accelerate development of innovative low-carbon technologies to reduce emissions and enhance international competitiveness.
reforms.component_name: Public R&D investment in climate and renewable energy
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Sectoral R&D investment in climate and energy technologies builds productive capacity, supports long-term competitiveness, and addresses market failures in green technology development.
reforms.status_evidence: Described as launched and implemented in 2008; funding allocation and programme structure explicitly stated.
reforms.importance_rationale: Structural, system-wide commitment of $30 billion over five years representing 0.6% of GDP; major sectoral R&D initiative with international technology transfer component.
reforms.source_quote: In June 2009, Japan established a medium-term target of reducing emissions by 15% from the 2005 level by 2020 (through domestic reductions alone) as a step to its long-term objective of cutting emissions by 60% to 80% by 2050. Price-based measures should be accompanied by other policy instruments... Public investment in R&D, particularly basic research, is important.

reforms.description: Japan increased outlays on education, science and technology as part of its fiscal stimulus packages in 2008-09, accounting for 7.2% of additional spending, intended as a supply-side measure to support both short-term demand and long-term growth potential.
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Counter-cyclical public R&D spending supports both immediate demand and long-term productivity growth through human capital and knowledge creation.
reforms.status_evidence: Described as part of fiscal stimulus packages in 2008-09; spending figures explicitly stated.
reforms.importance_rationale: Significant increase in R&D spending as part of broader fiscal stimulus, but narrower in scope than a dedicated sectoral programme.
reforms.source_quote: Outlays on education, science and technology are significant, accounting for 7.2% of the additional outlays.

reforms.description: Japan established a task force in 2007 and published an action programme in 2008 to accelerate medical device reviews and reduce time lags in the commercialisation of new medical devices. The government expanded PMDA (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency) capacity by increasing reviewers from 35 in 2008 to 104 by 2013, and from 200 in 2007 to more than 400 in 2010 through increased user fees, with recommendations to simplify information requirements, harmonise testing procedures with international standards, and reduce unnecessary re-testing.
reforms.component_name: PMDA capacity expansion and review process harmonisation
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Reducing regulatory review times and harmonising procedures with international standards lowers barriers to commercialisation of medical innovations, accelerates market entry, and enhances allocative efficiency in the medical device sector.
reforms.status_evidence: Task force established in 2007; action programme published in 2008; capacity expansion targets for 2010 and 2013 explicitly stated as implemented or in progress.
reforms.importance_rationale: Structural reform of regulatory infrastructure for medical devices; significant expansion of PMDA capacity and harmonisation with international standards; multi-year implementation (2007-2013).
reforms.source_quote: The key is for global companies to include Japan in their initial development of drugs... One positive step is the decision to increase the number of reviewers in the PMDA from 200 as of 2007 to more than 400 in 2010 by hiking user fees.

reforms.description: Japan implemented the Clinical Trial Activation Plan since 2003 to improve the cost, speed, and quality of clinical trials, with the goal of reducing barriers to drug development and accelerating the introduction of new drugs to the Japanese market.
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Reducing barriers and improving efficiency of clinical trials accelerates pharmaceutical innovation and market entry, supporting productivity growth in the health sector.
reforms.importance_rationale: Significant sectoral initiative to streamline clinical trial processes, but narrower in scope and budget than major R&D programmes.
reforms.source_quote: The government has also been implementing the 'Clinical Trial Activation Plan' since 2003 for improving the cost, speed and quality of clinical trials.

reforms.description: In 2004, Japan expanded the 'Specified Medical Costs' (SMC) list by adding 100 additional treatments and expanding the number of hospitals allowed to offer these treatments to approximately 2000, creating an exception to the ban on mixed billing to accelerate the adoption of advanced medical treatments under development.
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Expanding access to advanced medical treatments under development accelerates diffusion and adoption of medical innovations, supporting productivity growth in healthcare.
reforms.status_evidence: Described as expansion in 2004 with specific numbers of treatments and hospitals.
reforms.importance_rationale: Incremental expansion of an existing policy mechanism; narrower in scope than major sectoral R&D programmes.
reforms.source_quote: The debate over mixed billing led to a compromise in 2004 between the MHLW and the minister for regulatory reform to expand the list of treatments in the SMC... 100 additional treatments were added to the SMC and the number of hospitals allowed to offer these treatments was expanded to about 2000.

reforms.description: Japan launched a trial emissions trading system (ETS) in October 2008 that includes provisions for domestic crediting mechanisms allowing firms to claim CO2 reductions achieved through joint efforts with SMEs, supported by technology and finance from larger firms.
reforms.component_name: Domestic Crediting Mechanism for SME Technology Transfer
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: ETS creates incentives for technology development and knowledge transfer between firms (growth-supporting), but may impose compliance costs and distortions on firms (growth-hindering); net effect depends on design and carbon price level.
reforms.importance_rationale: Significant innovation instrument introducing market-based mechanisms for emissions reduction with technology transfer provisions, but described as a trial system with limited scope.
reforms.source_quote: The trial ETS allows participants to use Kyoto mechanism credits and domestic crediting mechanisms, which permit them to claim the CO2 reductions achieved through their joint efforts with small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Credits are created when SMEs achieve lower emissions...using technology and finance provided by large firms.

reforms.description: Japan should invest directly in basic R&D for energy-related technologies to share the risk of developing new technologies with the private sector and achieve innovations necessary to meet targeted emission reductions.
reforms.component_name: Direct public investment in energy R&D
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Public investment in basic energy R&D addresses market failures in fundamental research and supports long-term technological innovation.
reforms.status_evidence: Phrased as a recommendation ('should invest'); no evidence of government adoption or implementation.
reforms.importance_rationale: Recommendation or proposal not yet adopted; no specific budget or implementation timeline provided.
reforms.source_quote: Specific policies, in addition to price-based instruments, are needed therefore to foster R&D and the development of renewable energy sources. In particular, the government should invest directly in basic R&D to share the risk of developing new technologies with the private sector.

reforms.description: Japan's R&D on renewable energy more than doubled between 1996 and 2006, reflecting strategic investment in technological advancement for renewable energy sources, supporting the 2003 Renewable Portfolio Standard and the 2008 goal to increase zero-emission electricity generation.
reforms.growth_orientation_rationale: Strategic R&D investment in renewable energy technologies supports long-term productivity growth, technological competitiveness, and addresses market failures in clean energy innovation.
reforms.status_evidence: Described as historical investment trend between 1996 and 2006; supporting policies (2003 RPS, 2008 goal) explicitly stated.
reforms.importance_rationale: Significant sectoral R&D initiative with doubling of investment over a decade, but described as historical trend rather than a discrete policy reform.
reforms.source_quote: Although total R&D outlays on energy fell slightly between 1996 and 2006, Japan's R&D on renewables more than doubled over that period.
